     MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF ENTERGY TEXAS, INC.

       Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18

C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 213, Entergy Services, LLC (“Entergy Services”), on behalf of Entergy

Texas, Inc. (“Entergy Texas”) (Entergy Services and Entergy Texas collectively “Entergy”),

respectfully submits this motion for leave to answer and answer to the October 21, 2026 answer

filed by the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”), as corrected by its

October 22, 2026 errata, in the above-captioned dockets (“MISO Answer”).

       If approved by the Commission, MISO’s proposal to assign nearly $70 million in costs

from the Joint Targeted Interconnection Queue (“JTIQ”) upgrade projects (“JTIQ Upgrades”)

would increase rates for Entergy Texas customers who will not benefit from the upgrades.

Rejecting the proposed cost assignment will not adversely affect reliability, because the Lone

Star Power Station (“Lone Star”) can interconnect safely and reliably to MISO’s and Southwest

Power Pool, Inc.’s (“SPP”) systems whether the JTIQ Upgrades are in service or not; and the

JTIQ Upgrades will be fully funded even if Entergy Texas is appropriately excluded from the

group of JTIQ subscribers. Given the errors and unreasonable assumptions used by MISO in its

screening of Lone Star, the Commission should reject the proposed unexecuted JTIQ

Commitment Agreement (“JTIQ Agreement”) that MISO filed in Docket No. ER26-3558 and
 direct MISO to make minor conforming modifications to the unexecuted generator

interconnection agreement (“GIA”) filed in Docket No. ER26-3557, as discussed herein.



                                            MOTION

       The MISO Answer is the first time in which MISO attempts to support the proposed costs

that it seeks to impose upon Entergy Texas via the JTIQ Agreement (filed in Docket No. ER26-

3558), despite filing the JTIQ Agreement on August 19, 2026. Entergy respectfully seeks leave

to respond.

       Good cause exists to grant Entergy’s motion for leave to answer because, despite having

the opportunity and statutory obligation to support its Federal Power Act (“FPA”) section 205

application with its initial filing, MISO did not do so. Entergy has suffered prejudice due to

MISO’s failure to support its filing at the time it submitted the JTIQ Agreement. By withholding

its substantive arguments in support of its analyses from the record of these proceedings,

including the information offered by Sumit Pal Singh Brar in an affidavit (the “Brar Affidavit”),

until its answer, MISO deprived Entergy of the information needed to meaningfully respond to

the proposed cost allocation and its underlying basis. Due process considerations therefore

provide good cause for the Commission to accept this answer.

       Additionally, the Commission should accept this answer because it provides information

that will assist in the Commission’s decisionmaking. E.g., Tri-State Generation and

Transmission Ass’n, 185 FERC ¶ 61,201 at P 22 (2023), order on reh’g, 187 FERC ¶ 61,101

(2024). Specifically, it further clarifies how MISO has failed to implement its tariff in a manner

that is either reasonable or consistent with the representations it made to the Commission when it

originally proposed the JTIQ framework.




                                                 2
                                              ANSWER

       First, the biggest error in MISO’s answer is its contention that it has “appropriately

followed [MISO’s Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff

(‘MISO Tariff’)] and [the Joint Operating Agreement (‘JOA’) between MISO and

SPP] in screening the Lone Star Project for the JTIQ Participation Group.” MISO Answer at 7.

It has not. MISO’s assertion relies on logical fallacies and factual inaccuracies, and its actions

are not supported by the MISO Tariff. Entergy emphasizes that challenges to implementation of

tariff provisions, which Entergy raised in its protest filed on September 18, 2026 (the “Protest”),

are distinct from challenges to the tariff’s substantive terms, which Entergy did not raise in the

Protest. The filed rate doctrine does not insulate a Regional Transmission Organization’s

(“RTO”) misapplication of its tariff, nor does it prevent the Commission from reviewing whether

a transmission provider implemented tariff criteria reasonably. Entergy’s position in the Protest

concerns how MISO interpreted the MISO Tariff and implemented the JTIQ screens—not the

validity of the JTIQ framework itself.

       Second, MISO’s proffered legal defenses have no merit. Entergy is not seeking

preferential treatment. Entergy is asking that the Commission require MISO to implement its

tariff and the JOA in a just and reasonable manner in evaluating Lone Star. If MISO has been

misinterpreting its tariff and the JOA broadly, then there may be grounds for the Commission to

initiate a broader FPA section 206 inquiry. But the answer to Entergy’s evidence that MISO’s

flawed screening analysis fails the rough commensurability test—specifically with regard to

Lone Star—is not to accept an unjust and unreasonable cost assignment just because MISO may

also have used the same unreasonable screening assumptions for other projects. Under section

205 of the FPA, the Commission may not accept a rate that is unjust or unreasonable. 16 U.S.C.




                                                 3
 § 824d. Thus, the correct result here is for the Commission to reject the proposed cost

assignment to Lone Star and associated JTIQ Agreement. Furthermore, the JTIQ portfolio of

transmission projects is not expected to begin service for five years. The JTIQ framework allows

for an additional period of up to 20 years after that for MISO and SPP to complete their

screenings of qualifying generators, and MISO and SPP believe they have already identified

more than 44.5 GW that qualify, which is well over the target level of 28.6 GW. There is time

for MISO to get its novel screening analysis right, and no need to rush by assigning costs to the

wrong projects in contravention of the FPA.

       Third, MISO still has failed to meet its FPA section 205 burden of proof to demonstrate

that the proposed cost allocation to Lone Star is just and reasonable.

       Fourth, MISO’s interpretation of the screens is inconsistent with the Commission’s loop

flow precedent.

       Fifth, MISO’s Expedited Resource Addition (“ERAS”) arguments do not support its

unreasonable tariff interpretation, screening results, and cost allocation.

       Sixth, at a minimum, suspension and hearing proceedings remain warranted to resolve

significant questions of fact concerning MISO’s analyses.

       Seventh, the Commission should direct MISO to add to the GIA filed in Docket No.

ER26-3557 the minor clarification proposed by Entergy, because such clarification is necessary

to avoid confusion and the potential for conflicts between the interconnection agreement and the

JTIQ Agreement.




                                                  4
 I.     MISO Failed to Follow the Tariff When it Screened Lone Star

       A. MISO’s Unreasonable Interpretation and Implementation of the MISO Tariff
          Yields Absurd Results

       Throughout its answer, MISO attempts to frame its actions as consistent with the MISO

Tariff and argues that Entergy has offered “alternative methodologies” that it claims cannot be

squared with the tariff. E.g., MISO Answer at 16. MISO claims that “Entergy’s requested relief

seeks a new JTIQ methodology beyond what has been accepted by the Commission, which is

contrary to the filed rate and is an impermissible collateral attack on the accepted JTIQ

framework.” Id. at 7. In other words, MISO complains that some of Entergy’s positions about

the JTIQ screening analyses are not specifically included in the MISO Tariff.

       These arguments for incorrectly implementing the JTIQ screens are meritless. If MISO’s

method of tariff interpretation were followed to its logical conclusion, then arguably MISO has

performed all of its TARA-based interconnection studies incorrectly and in a manner that

violates its tariff. (TARA is powerflow software used by MISO.) For example, there is no

provision in the MISO Tariff that says MISO should apply a 70% loading filter for the flowgates

that it studies in any of the analyses it performs. Nonetheless, as Mr. Hudspeth has explained,

and as is set forth in MISO Business Practices Manual No. 15, the 70% loading criterion is one

that MISO adopted in order to evaluate the potential system impacts of Network Resource

Interconnection Service (“NRIS”) applications in both the traditional Definitive Planning Phase

(“DPP”) interconnection queue and in the ERAS process. This is because the 70% loading filter

ensures that MISO’s system impact studies identify material impacts—i.e., ones for which

transmission upgrades may be needed. Yet for purposes of the JTIQ, despite the reasonableness

of including the same assumption, MISO claims that the exact same assumption is not allowed,

even though nothing in the MISO Tariff or JOA prohibit it. Affidavit of Clayton Hudspeth at 6-8



                                                 5
 (attached hereto; “Hudspeth November Affidavit”). Like the use of the 70% criterion in the DPP

and ERAS processes, use of that criterion for JTIQ screening analyses is consistent with the

MISO Tariff and needed to provide reasonable results.

       MISO claims that it is following the “clear and unambiguous” language of the MISO

Tariff. MISO Answer at 12. But as discussed in the Protest, the MISO Tariff does not provide

clear instructions regarding implementation of the screening criteria. Protest at 23-24.

Moreover, MISO’s interpretation of the distribution factor screen fails the absurd results

doctrine. As the Commission has explained, “[i]t is . . . a well-settled principle of law that

agreements and tariffs are to be given a reasonable construction over one which results in unfair,

unusual, absurd, or improbable results.” AEP Generating Co., 39 FERC ¶ 61,158, 61,626 (1987)

(citing authorities). When the Commission approved the JTIQ framework, it did so based on

representations made by MISO about the purpose of the screens and expected outcomes. The

purpose of the screening methodology was to identify generating projects that are enabled by,

and thus will benefit from, the JTIQ portfolio of transmission projects. E.g., Midcontinent Indep.

Sys. Operator, Inc., 189 FERC ¶ 61,108 at P 67 (2024) (“JTIQ Order”), order on reh’g., 191

FERC ¶ 61,231 (2025) (“JTIQ Rehearing Order”). Yet, in Lone Star’s case, that is not so.

       It appears that the primary reason that MISO’s implementation of its screens has failed is

because MISO has elected to use an unreasonably broad definition of the SPP facilities on which

the 5% distribution factor criterion is applied. In doing so, MISO disregards the objective of that

screening criterion, which is to help identify if a generating project is enabled by and thus will

benefit from the JTIQ portfolio.

       The “DFAX impacts between 5.04% and 10.72% on five monitored elements in SPP’s

footprint” that MISO cites as the basis for Lone Star’s inclusion in the JTIQ Participation Group,




                                                  6
 MISO Answer at 12, occur on transmission lines located in SPP that have a maximum loading of

31%—a fact that Entergy already explained in its Protest. Protest at 35-36. Lone Star’s

distribution factor impacts on these lines in SPP are virtually identical whether the JTIQ

Upgrades are included in the model or excluded from the model. Id. at 36. In other words,

despite MISO’s assertions that Lone Star is “enabled” by the JTIQ portfolio, there is abundant

undisputed evidence to the contrary. Hudspeth November Affidavit at 2-3; Hudspeth September

Affidavit at 4-5, 45-50 (attached as Attachment 1 to the Protest). Rather than engage with this

evidence, MISO asserts that it does not matter because its screens show that Lone Star has “hit”

the threshold. But hitting a threshold that has been unreasonably defined does not demonstrate

enablement. Hudspeth November Affidavit at 37; contra MISO Answer at 15.

       Entergy is not aware of any interconnection analysis that would result in cost assignments

based on a screening criterion that is as broad as MISO has now interpreted the distribution

factor criterion to be. Moreover, when MISO and SPP originally proposed the screening criteria,

MISO gave no indication that a 5% distribution factor impact on any transmission line in SPP—

regardless of loading or location—would trigger a positive result for that screening element. To

the contrary, for example, MISO explained that “JTIQ’s methodology of adding a new

interconnection request to a model, identifying constraints caused, and then determining that

interconnection customer’s impact on the constraint using a distribution factor to assign cost

responsibility is a standard practice.” Transmittal Letter, Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator,

Inc., Docket No. ER24-2797-000 at 18 (filed on Aug. 16, 2024) (“JOA Transmittal Letter”)

(emphasis added). MISO also submitted testimony stating that “none of the JTIQ Upgrades

included in JTIQ Portfolio #1 would be needed but for the need to interconnect the JTIQ

Interconnection Customers assigned to that portfolio.” Testimony of Andrew Witmeier,




                                                 7
 Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Docket No. ER24-2871-000 at 14 (filed on Aug. 26,

2024) (“Witmeier Testimony”). Thus it was reasonable for Entergy and the Commission to

understand that the “facilities of the potentially impacted Party’s transmission system”

referenced in the MISO Tariff would be facilities that are relevant to the objectives of the JTIQ

portfolio. MISO Tariff, Attachment X Section 3.5.1.1(2). In the same way, even though

MISO’s Tariff does not specify precisely how a system impact study is supposed to be

performed, we reasonably understand that it is not a study for a 5% impact on any facility

regardless of the facility’s loading. MISO’s interpretation of the distribution factor screen is

unreasonably broad and yields absurd results. It fails to advance the purpose of the JTIQ

framework, and the Commission should not accept the proposed cost assignment to Lone Star

based on it.

       Rather, the correct way for MISO to have implemented the screens set forth in the MISO

Tariff would have been to identify the relevant “facilities” of SPP. This is analogous to how

MISO identifies relevant flowgates in the standard interconnection analyses, even though that

step of the interconnection study process is nowhere to be found in the MISO Tariff. Here, the

relevant facilities are congested or heavily-loaded facilities. As Mr. Hudspeth explains in his

September Affidavit, there were at least two options, and MISO could have identified another

reasonable option. Hudspeth September Affidavit at 50-52. But it goes against the very

foundations of cost causation principles to suggest that a greater than 5% distribution factor

impact on an unconstrained and lightly-loaded facility that will not be relieved by the JTIQ

Upgrades is somehow a relevant criterion for assigning JTIQ project costs.

       MISO’s interpretation of its tariff is plainly unreasonable, and that is at least one reason

why the JTIQ screening results for Lone Star should be rejected as invalid. And, again, MISO’s




                                                  8
 claim that it cannot perform the JTIQ screening studies to screen for congested facilities that will

be impacted by an interconnecting generator is inconsistent with its own use of the 70% loading

criterion in the DPP and ERAS processes.

       B. MISO’s Implementation of the Screening Analysis Utilizes Multiple Elective
          Assumptions and Criteria That the Tariff Does Not Mandate

       MISO argues that the context of the MISO Tariff is not relevant based on its

interpretation of the “plain” language. MISO Answer at 13-14, 19-20. As discussed above,

MISO’s interpretation of the “plain” language is not reasonable and yields absurd results.

       Furthermore, the screening test that MISO and SPP proposed for the JTIQ framework

was not proposed in a vacuum. Instead, it was proposed in the context of the interconnection

study process—which is indeed what MISO attempts to leverage to support the choices it made

in implementing the screens.

       Mr. Brar repeatedly asserts that MISO has used the “same” models and input files as

those that are used for the system impact studies it performs. E.g., Brar Affidavit at 14, 24, 25.

There is at least one key difference, however, in how MISO performs other system impact

studies and the JTIQ screening studies. When, in response to a request for NRIS, MISO

performs an Interconnection System Impact Study, which is defined as “an engineering study

that evaluates the impact of the proposed interconnection on the safety and reliability of

Transmission System and, if applicable, an Affected System,” MISO Tariff, Attachment X,

Section 1, MISO does not evaluate the impact of the proposed interconnection on all facilities.

Instead, it restricts the analysis to flowgates that are loaded at 70% or greater. Notably, the

words “constrained” or “heavily loaded” are not in the definition of “Interconnection System

Impact Study” either. In other words, even though it is standard practice for MISO to evaluate

the impacts of proposed interconnections on constrained or heavily-loaded facilities in its



                                                  9
 interconnection studies, that concept is not explicitly set forth in the MISO Tariff. Its absence in

the JTIQ provisions of the tariff thus does not carry the significance that MISO suggests.

        In order to perform the JTIQ screens, however, MISO directs the power flow software to

include the results of facilities loaded at zero or very low levels. Hudspeth November Affidavit

at 7. The MISO Tariff language cited by MISO does not “require” this approach. Again, it

would have been reasonable for MISO to retain the flowgate loading filters that it applies in the

normal course of its interconnection studies (i.e., the 70% loading filter). And MISO gave no

explicit indication in its JTIQ framework proposal that it had planned to depart from this

assumption. To the contrary, MISO clearly stated that its JTIQ screening would be based on

identifying constraints caused by an interconnecting generating facility. E.g., JOA Transmittal

Letter at 18.

        Mr. Brar attempts to argue that the 70% loading filter is not relevant for JTIQ screening,

because it is only used “to quickly identify potentially impactful flowgates” in the NRIS process.

Brar Affidavit at 23. But this simply amounts to an admission that MISO’s choice to screen all

SPP facilities for Lone Star, rather than those that are relevant to the question of whether Lone

Star is enabled by the JTIQ Upgrades, includes SPP facilities that are not potentially impactful.

See Hudspeth November Affidavit at 7-8. This departure “conflicts with these general principles

and practice” regarding the identification of customers who benefit from transmission system

upgrades. Id. Had MISO used the standard 70% loading filter here, Lone Star would not have

been screened into the JTIQ Participation Group. Id. at 6.

        Additionally, as Mr. Hudspeth originally pointed out in his September 2026 affidavit,

MISO utilized a number of assumptions in developing the JTIQ screens. These include the

reference subsystem and the contingencies that would be monitored. Hudspeth September




                                                 10
 Affidavit at 28-32, 36-38. Mr. Brar asserts that these are the same as what MISO uses for other

studies, e.g., Brar Affidavit at 24, but as Mr. Hudspeth explains, that is not true for certain

assumptions, like the monitoring files that are unique to JTIQ. Hudspeth November Affidavit at

5-7. Moreover, even if the claim were accurate, it does not mean that the chosen assumptions

were reasonable, especially in light of MISO’s choice to change the flowgate loading criterion.

For example, MISO does not explain why it is reasonable to use MISO’s set of contingencies to

analyze effects on the SPP system, rather than the set of contingencies that SPP uses in Affected

System Studies, when the purpose of the JTIQ screens is to replace the SPP Affected System

Studies. Id. at 31. And, critically, none of those flawed assumptions used by MISO are grounded

in the MISO Tariff. Mr. Hudspeth addresses Mr. Brar’s responses to the unreasonable

assumptions in his attached affidavit, and he explains why Mr. Brar’s responses do not resolve

his concerns. See id. at 7-31.

       In light of the MISO Tariff’s absence of direction with regard to the JTIQ screens, two of

the erroneous assumptions raised by Mr. Hudspeth are worth emphasizing. First, MISO ignores

the load associated with ERAS projects. Hudspeth September Affidavit at 28-32. MISO touted

the ERAS process as narrowly tailored, and the Commission approved the ERAS process as

such, in part because each generator must have an associated resource adequacy need located in

the same, pre-defined local resource zone where it will be built. Midcontinent Indep. Sys.

Operator, Inc., 192 FERC, ¶ 61,064 at PP 37, 81, 195, 210-12 (2025), aff’d, 194 FERC ¶ 61,050

at PP 57-58 (2026). The ERAS process also required, for Entergy Texas and most other ERAS

applicants, a verification by the relevant electric retail regulatory authority confirming the

relationship between the associated resource adequacy need and the generator. Recently, the

Commission also recognized that new generation that is sited electrically proximate to new large




                                                  11
 loads can limit the impacts to the transmission system of interconnecting that generation.

Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,212 at P 113 (2026). Yet despite the

fact that ERAS projects are unique and that MISO could perform the JTIQ screen in a manner

that would recognize the unique resource adequacy service they provide, MISO elected to

perform the screens in a manner that ignores the relationship between Lone Star and the

electrically proximate loads within Entergy Texas’s service area that it is being built to serve.

This decision is unreasonable, and it is not mandated by the MISO Tariff.

       As Mr. Hudspeth explained, MISO would not have reached the inaccurate distribution

factor results that it did if it had corrected the reference subsystem to use Entergy Texas load and

thereby accurately reflect the relationship between Lone Star and the loads it is serving in

Southeast Texas. Hudspeth September Affidavit at 32. Lone Star is being constructed to serve

significant load growth in Texas, but these customers will not benefit from the JTIQ Upgrades.

And one of Entergy Texas’s large customers—Golden Pass LNG Terminal LLC—has protested

MISO’s proposed JTIQ cost assignment precisely because it recognizes that the JTIQ Upgrades

will not provide any tangible benefits to Lone Star or its customers. Joint Motion to Intervene

and Protest of Golden Pass LNG Terminal LLC, Golden Pass LNG Marine Services LLC, and

Golden Pass Pipeline LLC, Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Docket No. ER26-3558

(filed on Sept. 17, 2026). If MISO had used the correct reference subsystem in recognition of

Lone Star’s documented and expected power transfers to these new Entergy Texas loads, Lone

Star would not have triggered the distribution factor screen within the JTIQ screening criteria.

       Second, MISO still has not offered any Tariff, JOA, or Business Practices Manual-based

support for the method it used to study the impacts of Lone Star on the Sibley upgrade. MISO’s

response is that monitoring “all lines in and out of the Sibley bus . . . accurately represents the




                                                  12
 MW impacts on the Sibley bus.” MISO Answer at 22. As Mr. Hudspeth explains at length, this

is not correct, because it fails to consider whether the Sibley upgrade itself is impacted.

Hudspeth November Affidavit at 19-26. Again, MISO has not explained how its study of

existing lines satisfies the MISO Tariff requirement to study the JTIQ upgrade. Nor has MISO

provided the actual details of the Sibley upgrade that are necessary in order for study of the

upgrade to occur. Instead, it has continued to defend its non-Tariff study, which as Mr. Hudspeth

explains, “is another indication … that MISO’s overall approach to the JTIQ screening process is

not reliable.” Id. at 26.

        In short, MISO’s use of elective assumptions in implementing its screens in a manner that

is contrary to the objectives of the JTIQ framework and other Commission policies is not

protected by the Tariff, JOA, or Business Practices Manual, and it is not just and reasonable. Its

screening results do not afford a reliable basis upon which to assign $70 million in upgrade costs.

        C. MISO’s Unreasonable Interpretation of the Tariff and Revisionist History
           Departs From What it Told the Commission When it Proposed the JTIQ
           Framework

        The Commission approved the JTIQ framework because MISO and SPP said that it

would allow for the “interconnection of a certain MW amount of generation capacity along the

MISO-SPP seam[.].” JTIQ Order, 189 FERC ¶ 61,108 at P 213 n.476 (emphasis added). MISO

and SPP also said—and the Commission approved the JTIQ framework because—the JTIQ

transmission projects “are aimed at addressing transmission system limitations preventing the

interconnection of large amounts of generation, particularly location-constrained renewable

generation resources.” Id. at P 94. In approving the JTIQ framework, the Commission was told

that it would enable the interconnection of new generation at the MISO-SPP seam.

        Lone Star is not at the seam; nor is it electrically close to the parts of the seam that are

constrained or limited. It is not a location-constrained renewable resource. Its interconnection is


                                                  13
 not physically challenged due to existing (or any identified future) transmission system

limitations. Lone Star is sited in close proximity to the load growth it will serve. The fact that

MISO has interpreted the screens in a way that cause Lone Star to “hit the threshold” does not

mean that Lone Star is “enabled.” Contra MISO Answer at 15. It means something is wrong

with the screening analysis.

       MISO also now tells the Commission that Lone Star’s impacts “were significant, which is

consistent with Lone Star’s expected MW output as a large-size natural gas-fired generating

facility.” Id. at 18. Mr. Brar asserts that he was not surprised Lone Star was included in the

JTIQ Participation Group. Brar Affidavit at 17. He states that “Lone Star is a very large natural

gas-fired combustion turbine. Such a large addition is expected to have significant system

impacts.” Id. This is the exact same thing he said about Entergy Texas’s Legend Power Station

(“Legend”), which is a generator that is requesting 65% more megawatts of interconnection

service than Lone Star.

       This is also a surprising assertion itself. In his affidavit, Mr. Brar adopts as his own

testimony the prior testimony of Andrew Witmeier in Docket No. ER24-2797-000 (the “Brar

Adopted Testimony”). Id. at 10. In what is now his testimony, Mr. Brar explained that an

Expanded Scope Analysis applies to interconnection requests (a) included in the JTIQ

Participation Group and (b) that do not meet the criteria for inclusion in the JTIQ Participation

Group and are not located in MISO South. Brar Adopted Testimony at 27. He also explained

that interconnection requests for generation located in MISO South that do not meet the criteria

for inclusion in the JTIQ Participation Group are included in the SPP Affected System Process.

Id. at 28. In the testimony he adopted as his own, Mr. Brar further explained that the exception to

the Expanded Scope Analysis for MISO South (and SPP Groups 4 and 5) “is based on where the




                                                 14
 JTIQ Portfolio is not expected to enable generation. The RTOs anticipate proposing a future

portfolio to address the needs of the currently excepted regions.” Id. at 29.

        In other words, in testimony he adopted as his own, Mr. Brar stated that the JTIQ

Portfolio is not expected to enable generation in MISO South. In that same docket, MISO stated

in its transmittal letter that “[i]t is possible that an interconnection request interconnecting to the

most northern part of MISO South or SPP Zones 4 and 5 could meet the criteria for inclusion in

the Participation Group.” JOA Transmittal Letter at 21 n.98. At the same time, Mr. Brar now

argues that he was not surprised that Lone Star—which is in the most southern part of MISO

South—is in the JTIQ Participation Group, a claim directly at odds with his and MISO’s prior

statements.

        Even if Lone Star were expected to have “significant system impacts” (and Mr. Hudspeth

explains in his September 2026 affidavit why that is not the case, e.g., Hudspeth September

Affidavit at 12-13, 45-50), that fact alone would not show that the JTIQ Upgrades themselves

would benefit Lone Star. MISO’s screening results for other ERAS projects demonstrate this to

be true. In ERAS cycles 1 through 3, multiple “large” natural gas-fired projects (e.g., E0010,

E0012, E0016, and E0042, all over 790 MW) did not trigger the JTIQ screens. Compare

MISO’s list of ERAS projects, available at

https://cdn.misoenergy.org/ERAS%20Interconnection%20Requests718481.pdf?v=20250925100

448, with JTIQ dashboard indicating screened-in projects by cluster, available at

https://app.powerbigov.us/view?r=eyJrIjoiMDZkMWZkOGEtNzNjMy00MDU0LWI4YjUtNmZ

jMjdlMzFiZWI1IiwidCI6IjYwNDA5MTViLTlkZmYtNGQ0Ny1iYjM1LThhYzljOWE1ZGMxO

CJ9 (last accessed November 3, 2026).




                                                  15
        Finally, MISO told the Commission that the generators that would be screened into the

JTIQ Participation Group would be enabled by, and thus benefit from, the JTIQ projects. E.g.,

JTIQ Rehearing Order, 191 FERC ¶ 61,231 at P 12 n.35 (Commission explaining that MISO and

SPP asserted that interconnection requests that meet the JTIQ screening criteria “are those that

impact the affected RTO’s system and are enabled by the JTIQ Portfolio”). However, the

multiple additional analyses that Mr. Hudspeth provided with his September 2026 affidavit

demonstrate that is not true for Lone Star. Notably, MISO does not appear to dispute the validity

of these analyses. MISO attempts to dismiss the relevance of the Affected System Study because

it is not the same thing as the screens. MISO Answer at 28. But Mr. Hudspeth’s additional

analyses and his assessment of the likely Affected System Study results are all relevant because

they demonstrate how disconnected MISO’s implementation of the screens is from the purpose

of the JTIQ framework. They offer useful “additional information about both Lone Star’s effects

on the SPP system and the effects of the JTIQ Upgrades on the SPP system impacted by Lone

Star,” and they affirmatively show that “the JTIQ Upgrades do not benefit Lone Star.” Hudspeth

November Affidavit at 39. Put simply, MISO still has not shown (and cannot show) that Lone

Star in fact will be enabled by the JTIQ Upgrades, and thus it has not demonstrated that Lone

Star will benefit from those projects.

       MISO’s tariff interpretation and its implementation of the JTIQ screens are not
